title: Interfaces & Abstraction: Program to a Contract, Not an Implementation
oneLiner: Calling code that only knows about an interface never needs to change when a new implementation shows up -- this app is a live example of exactly that.
keyTakeaway: "Program to an interface, not an implementation" means the code that USES an object should only depend on WHAT it can do (its interface), never on HOW it does it or WHICH concrete class it happens to be -- which is the actual mechanism behind this app's own IConcept/ITool design letting every lesson be added as one new file, touching nothing else.
explanation:
An INTERFACE is a contract: a list of methods (and their signatures: each method's name, parameters and return type) that a class promises to implement, with zero information about HOW. Code that depends only on the interface -- "give me something that satisfies IAnimal" -- never needs to know or care whether it's actually holding a Dog, a Cat, or a Duck, only that whatever it's holding has a MakeSound() method. That's ABSTRACTION: hiding the concrete details behind a shared, simpler surface.

The value shows up the moment a NEW implementation appears. Code written against the interface keeps working, unmodified, for every class that satisfies it -- past, present, and future. Try it below: the SAME calling function (shown underneath) runs unchanged no matter which animal you pick, because it was written against IAnimal, not against Dog specifically.

This app is its own real example, not just a toy one: every practice lesson implements IConcept, every reference lesson implements ITool (see content/IConcept.cs and ITool.cs), and the exporter that turns lessons into the site's files is written against those interfaces. None of them contain a single line of code that knows about BstInsert or PlcScanCycle by name. That's exactly why this app could keep growing one brand-new lesson at a time as "one new file, nothing else touched": the same property adding a Triangle demonstrated in OOP Basics, at the scale of an entire application instead of one function.
